31.21.2.en: * Since bodily works are accomplished by the shoulder and the arm, he wished his shoulder to fall and his arm to be broken into pieces if he spoke with his mouth of good things without practicing them in deed.

31.22.0.en: “For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure” [23].

31.22.1.en: After speaking of his exceeding tenderness toward all the deprived classes, and his esteem for all who were rejected by society, even the slaves, he lifts his eyes with all reverence toward God and wonders why God allowed him to suffer these harsh trials.

31.22.2.en: When Job felt the weight of the afflictions he was filled with terror, and felt that the hand of God had become heavy upon him.

31.23.s.en: 11. His trust is in God, not in his wealth

31.23.0.en: 24 “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence; 25 If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much;

31.23.1.en: “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [24].

31.23.2.en: Had he relied on his wealth and possessions, there would have been a reason for all this to be taken from his hand. But he had focused all his feelings, emotions and intentions on the Creator and not on the creature, so why were these blessings taken from him?

31.23.3.en: * It happens that a man stops placing his hope in the Creator, so that hope in the creature takes His place.

31.23.4.en: That rich man fixed his hope on uncertain things when he said: [Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry] (Lk 12:19). But the voice from on high rebuked him, saying: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Lk 12:20)... For God stands forever, and all these things pass away. What, then, is this, that we fly from Him who alone stands, and cling to passing things?

31.24.0.en: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much” [25].

31.24.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that the victory won by righteous Job during his trial was not the product of the moment, but the fruit of practical spiritual training that he lived by divine grace even before the trial came, among which was his training in despising temporal blessings and earthly wealth.

31.24.2.en: * Such was blessed Job. Had he not trained himself well before entering the struggles, he would not have shone in splendor in this way. Had he not experienced freedom from despondency, he would have uttered words in a rush when his sons died. But as he was before, so he stood against all the assaults: against the destruction of his wealth and the great ruin that came upon him, against the loss of his sons, the consolation of his wife, the plague that struck his body, the reproaches of his friends, and the insults of his servants.

31.24.3.en: If you also want to see his ways on the (spiritual) path, listen to him telling how he despised wealth, saying: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, if I gathered gold in huge quantities, if I trusted in precious stones” (Job 31:25, 24) LXX. Therefore he was not troubled when he lost these things, because he did not desire them when he had them.

31.24.4.en: * Job was rich, but he did not serve the demon of greed, mammon; rather he reigned over wealth and mastered it, so he was a lord and not a slave. Therefore he possessed all these things as a steward of another’s money, not only not seizing from others, but giving what was his to the needy. And what is more, when he had these possessions they did not make him glad, for he declared, saying: [If I rejoiced when my wealth was great] (Job 31:25), nor did he grieve when they were gone from him.

31.24.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * The saints, in this pitiable journey, long for that appearing of their Creator which they cannot now contemplate, and so they count the whole fullness of the present life as if it were poverty. Nothing outside God satisfies the mind that truly seeks after God.

31.24.6.en: Such persons often count abundant goods an excessive burden, for they carry many things with seriousness while they hasten toward their homeland. Therefore they devote their energy so that their needy relatives may share with them...

31.24.7.en: The elect will not rejoice in many goods, because out of love for the heavenly inheritance they give away and distribute what is in their hands, despising it and renouncing it.

31.25.0.en: 26 If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness; 27 And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand: 28 This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above.

31.25.1.en: “If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness” [26].

31.25.2.en: As his wealth was not his trust, but the Giver of wealth, so the sun and the moon, with their beauty and splendor, took no place in his heart; rather he was enlightened by God, the Creator of the sun and the moon, the true eternal Light.

31.25.3.en: The sun and the moon were objects of worship for many in the days of Job, who honored them as soldiers of heaven. This act was counted the height of evil and ingratitude toward God the Creator.

31.25.4.en: * Job tells us that he did not look at the sun as it rose, nor at the moon as it walked in brightness, showing that he did not seek the present light.

31.25.5.en: As the soul pours itself out in contemplation outside itself, so much the more does it do so in order to return to inward things. Thus all who have wise hearts avoid falling toward outward things through the bodily senses. Instead they make continual effort to gather themselves within by hidden discipline, guarding their own selves, so as to be found wholly in what is inward.

31.25.6.en: Jeremiah bound himself to the depths of his heart in earnest discipline, and fled from longing for the outward life, when he said: [I did not desire the day of man, thou knowest] (cf. Jer 17:16).

31.25.7.en: * Just as the “gold” of understanding did not make Job proud, so also the light of outward works did not make him exalt himself before the eyes of men...

31.25.8.en: The sun in its brightness is the good works displayed outwardly. It is written: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16). Again: “Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning” (Lk 12:35). For what is said in this passage about the rising sun means the Gospel, which is indicated by the burning lamps. When good works shine among unbelievers, the lamp is lit in the night; and when they shine in the Church, the sun shines in the day.

31.25.10.en: * Many have strayed from the One in many ways. Some deified the sun, so that when it set they dwell at night without a god.

31.25.11.en: And some worshiped the moon, so that they have no god by day.

31.25.12.en: And some worshiped the parts of the rest of the world.

31.25.14.en: And some worshiped various kinds of foods, and some their pleasures, and some took delight in women, so they set up a statue of a naked woman and called her Aphrodite, and worshiped their lusts in a visible form.

31.25.15.en: And some were dazzled by the glitter of gold and worshiped it, and others worshiped other kinds of these things.

31.26.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem “And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand” [27].

31.26.1.en: Righteous Job affirms that idols, gold, precious stones and abundant wealth could not, all of them, deceive his heart in secret; that is, not only did he not practice any kind of arrogance, pride or idolatry in deed, but none of it even crept stealthily into his heart.

31.26.2.en: Putting the hand to the mouth and kissing it is a custom practiced by many when their hearts are occupied with something very dear to them or when they greatly admire it, and so they express what is in their hearts by sending kisses from the mouth through the hand, pointing to whom or what they love. Thus neither wealth nor idols occupied him, nor did he love these things, nor send them his kisses.

31.26.3.en: * Stretching the hand to the mouth is the harmony between voice and practice. He who praises what he does kisses his hand with his mouth, and so bears witness to his speech by the merits of his practical deeds. In this case, who is the despiser if not the one who receives the very same gifts for doing them (and ascribes them to himself)? The great Preacher says well: “What hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1 Cor 4:7). Now the saints themselves know that they are of the stock of a corrupt origin, since from the fall of our first father it is grace that changes us for the better in desires and works... They perceive that they have received strength for the struggle. So blessed Job tells of the good things that he practices, but he never ascribes them to his own work. On the contrary, he praises his Creator, and denies that he kissed his hand with his mouth.

31.27.0.en: “This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above” [28].

31.27.1.en: The love of the world did not creep into Job’s heart, nor did idol worship creep into it. Had he fallen into either, he would have deserved what came upon him as a divine punishment. He did not deny his God by clinging to creation or by deifying it.

31.28.s.en: 13. No thought of gloating enters him

31.28.0.en: 29 “If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: 30 Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul.

31.28.1.en: “If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him” [29].

31.28.2.en: Job was careful not to deny his Creator, nor to wrong his brother or hate him, even if his brother hated him. No thought of gloating over an opponent or one who hated him crept into his mind. Solomon the Wise says: “Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: Lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him” (Prov 24:17-18).

31.28.3.en: * The ways of the wicked who devise harm are death (Prov 12:28). “Thou shalt not devise harm against thy brother” (Lev 19:18) LXX. And also: [If you see the ass of him that hateth you fallen (in the mire), you shall not pass by it until you have first lifted it up] (Ex 23:5). On this point each one must bear in mind that he may not leave his enemy’s ass in the mire, so how can a man hate or ignore a human being created in the image of God?

31.28.4.en: I have noticed in blessed Job a true, perfect love, in all faithfulness, even toward his enemies, so that he could rejoice and say with a clear conscience to the Lord: [If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him, and said in my heart: Well done!] (Job 31:29-30).

31.28.5.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Keeping love is the only proof that we are disciples of Almighty God. The Truth says: “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Jn 13:35).

31.28.6.en: This love, if it truly fills our hearts, is usually shown in two ways: we love our friends in God, and we love our enemies for God’s sake...

31.28.7.en: If we rejoice at the misfortunes of one who hates us, it is clear that we do not love him, since we do not wish him to be better than ourselves...

31.29.0.en: “Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul” [30].

31.29.1.en: Not only did he not stir himself to harm the one who hated him, nor gloat when distress or disaster came upon him, but he did not dare to ask God against his brother. He did not seek vengeance on those who harmed him, nor did a word of cursing come out of his mouth against them!

31.29.2.en: * Those who attack an enemy with curses, what do they want God to do to him but what they are unable to do, or are ashamed to do...? In that same place, did those who read “Love your enemies” not also read “Bless, and curse not”? Again: “Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing” (Lk 6:27; Rom 12:14; 1 Pet 3:9).

31.30.s.en: 14. Marvelous love for the people of his household

31.30.0.en: 31 “If the men of my tabernacle said not, Who will bring one who has not been satisfied with his food? 32 The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.

31.30.1.en: “If the men of my tabernacle said not:

31.30.2.en: Who will bring one who has not been satisfied with his food?” [31]

31.30.3.en: Job’s nature was wonderful: he gave continually and generously, especially to the needy and the poor, giving others their needs not merely to the point of sufficiency but until they were satisfied. This was a cause of amazement to the people of his tent; even the hired servants, the slaves and the maidservants marveled at his tenderness toward all. He was admired by everyone who dealt with him!

31.30.4.en: This saying points to the Savior, whom the men of His tent, or His Church, long to have enter, that each one may enjoy the Body of the Lord and be spiritually satisfied by it, whether of the persecuting Jews or of the Gentiles who accept the faith.

31.30.5.en: St. John Chrysostom comments on what is said here: [Oh, that we were filled with his flesh!], that this is an expression of the intense love binding Job to his servants, and that the Lord Christ gives us His Body to eat as a declaration of the intense love between Him and His believers: [This Body He gives us to eat, which befits intense love. For those who have warmth in their hearts, we often bite with our teeth. Therefore Job, pointing to the love of his servants for him, said that they often did this because of their strong affection for him, saying: ‘Oh, that we were filled with his flesh!’ (see Job 31:31). So Christ gives us to be filled with His Body, drawing us to a greater love.]

31.30.6.en: * [If I have allowed the poor man to go out of my house empty-handed] [31]. He did not say “I gave when he begged,” but “I gave even to the one who refused to take.” Those who entered his house had to leave only after receiving... Job used pressure on those he gave to, so that they would take.

31.30.7.en: * This too Christ does, to lead us to close friendship and to show His love for us, for He gives those who long for Him not only to see Him, but also to touch Him, to eat Him, to fix their teeth in His flesh, to embrace Him, and to satisfy all their love. Let us return from that table like lions breathing fire, becoming a terror to Satan, thinking of our Head and of the love He shows us.

31.30.8.en: St. John Chrysostom “The stranger did not lodge in the street.”

31.31.0.en: “I opened my doors to the traveller” [32].

31.31.1.en: St. Ambrose offers us a symbolic interpretation, seeing in the true believer one who imitates Job and brings those who are strangers to the faith into his house, which is the Church of God.

31.31.2.en: Righteous Job is a type of the Lord Christ, and his house is a type of the Church. The Lord Christ longs for the doors of His Church to be opened so that every stranger may enter it. All are washed by His precious Blood, enjoy the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and become members of the household of God. If all humanity is a caravan ever on the move, then the doors of God’s mercies are open to them, that they may enjoy the blessings of God’s saving work during their journey in this world.

31.31.3.en: * Take away good will from men and it is like taking the sun from the world. Without it men no longer care to show the way to the stranger, or to bring back the one who has strayed, or to show generosity. This is no small virtue. Because of it Job praised himself, saying: [The stranger did not lodge (outside my gates), I opened my door to the traveller] (Job 31:32)... Thus good will is found in all these things, like a spring of water that refreshes the thirsty, and like a light that shines on others and does not withhold its brightness from those who give light to others.

31.31.4.en: St. Ambrose * He says: I gave generously to every needy person. I offered my roof that they might share it with me. When I noticed that they were in a public place, I offered my house, my table, and all that I had to be held in common. I counted myself as a treasurer for the needy, without looking on my possessions as personal property, but as the property of the Master (the Lord). “The LORD gave” (Job 1:21), and accordingly let us be partners with all His servants.

31.31.5.en: * Poverty and wealth are two similar weapons, with which we serve virtue if we wish... To learn that this is true, let us recall the case of Job, who became rich and also poor, and used these two weapons in a similar way, conquering with both. When he was rich he said: [I opened my door to every traveller] (Job 31:32). And when he became poor he said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good in His eyes, so He has done” [(Job 1:21) LXX and the Vulgate]. When he was rich he showed generous hospitality, and when he was poor he showed much patience.

31.31.6.en: * Not only what we give as alms, but also what we bear steadfastly when others rob us of what is ours, both of these yield us great fruit. And that you may know that the latter is truly greater, I offer as witness what befell Job. When he possessed wealth he opened his house to the poor, giving them what he had. But he was not as famous when he opened his house to the poor as he became when he heard that his house had fallen and did not receive the news with a troubled heart. He did not gain fame when he clothed the naked with the fleece of his sheep, as he became famous and known when he heard that fire had fallen on his flocks and burned them all, and yet gave thanks. Before, he was a lover of men; now he became a lover of wisdom. Before, he was compassionate to the poor; now he gives thanks to the Lord... He knew that God was ordering all things for good.

31.32.0.en: “If I covered my transgressions as men do, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom” [33].

31.32.1.en: A beautiful picture of the humility of righteous Job. For with all the preceding amazing traits of a man living in the midst of a pagan world, who holds fast to his Creator, into whose heart the love of possessions does not creep, but who gives and bestows with marvelous generosity, and esteems and honors even the male and female slaves, he does not deny that he has faults and sins; he does not hide them in his bosom but confesses them openly.

31.32.2.en: * These are the proofs of true humility, that a man affirms his own evil, confirming it by disclosing it with the voice of confession. This is contrary to the habit of the human race, that a man practices sin while keeping himself hidden from sight. And when it is discovered he denies it, hiding it, and when he is accused of it he multiplies his sins by falling into defending himself. Since the fall of man we have been drawn down to these degrees of evil... And as the sin of concealment grew, it reached a frightful extent in the human race, and blessed Job said: [If I hid my transgressions], adding the words “as a man,” since he saw that taking the likeness of the first parents had become a pattern for man...

31.32.3.en: Blessed Job displayed a singular humility, for he knew that he lived among adversaries, and yet he did not fear to disclose his faults with the voice of confession. Note that he first tells of his virtuous traits, and after that confesses his sin.

31.32.5.en: * He was not turned aside by the crowds of the people, that is, those subject to him, who knew his natural faults. This indeed is wisdom: [Confess first your transgressions, that you may be justified] (cf. Isa 43:26). Thus I have not taken anyone as a witness to my good works, while I wish everyone to know my faults and transgressions. This is the height of wisdom, a pattern of virtue, that a person hide his good works and expose his faults to the public. In any case, this is contrary to what is practiced in reality.

31.32.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. Thus you become like a righteous man who accuses himself at the start of his speech in court, or like Job, whom the crowd of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his offense before all.

31.33.s.en: 16. The clans rise up against him without cause

31.33.0.en: “Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me, that I kept silence, and went not out of the door?” [34]

31.33.1.en: Although he was accustomed to confess his sins openly and not conceal them within him, the situation had completely changed, for the tribes had risen up against him, and it was as though the clans had no work but violent attack against him, without cause. As for him, he did not allow his mouth to utter anything for a time. His words became like words that do not go out of the door of his mouth.

31.33.2.en: * It is as though he says plainly: While others did not cease attacking me outwardly, I myself remained free from disturbance within my soul. For what are we to take the door to be here but the mouth? By it we come forward, as it were, to disclose the secrets of our hearts. While we remain within in the conscience, we go out through the tongue.

31.33.3.en: But there are some who fear above all to be despised, and aim to appear wise when accused of deserving contempt...

31.33.4.en: When the saints are on trial, they abstain completely from appearing (to defend themselves), and when they cannot benefit those who listen to them, they keep silence, even to be despised, lest they boast by displaying their wisdom... It is written: [And when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceeding glad: for he was desirous to see him of a long season, because he had heard many things of him; and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him]. And I add: “Then he questioned with him in many words; but he answered him nothing.” But how greatly the Lord was despised because He kept silence was shown by the words that follow immediately: “And Herod with his men of war set him at nought, and mocked him” (Lk 23:8-9, 11).

31.33.5.en: It befits us to hear and learn that those who listen to us often want to be known through matters that concern us, and not that they may correct their faults. Therefore it befits us to hold to silence, lest, if we speak the word of God openly, the faults of these persons do not cease, and we ourselves sin...

31.33.6.en: The Preacher says: “For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ” (2 Cor 2:17)... To speak as of sincerity is to seek nothing beyond what is necessary and needful...

31.33.7.en: He speaks as of God who knows that he himself has nothing of his own, but speaks only what he receives from God. He speaks in the sight of God who does not seek what belongs to men in all that he utters, but is occupied with the presence of Almighty God, and looks toward the glory of his Creator, not his own glory.

31.34.0.en: 35 “Oh that one would hear me! behold, here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me, and that mine adversary had written a complaint. 36 Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, and bind it as a crown to me. 37 I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him. 38 If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain; 39 If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life: 40 Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley.” The words of Job are ended.

31.34.4.en: And that mine adversary had written a complaint” [35].

31.34.5.en: In the end Job returns to ask what he had asked before, repeating his request to find someone who would enter into a trial with him and hear him. He himself signed the request to enter into the trial, and to be ready to accept whatever punishment he deserves.

31.34.6.en: He asks that the Almighty Himself, the Searcher of hearts and reins and the Knower of secrets, rise up to judge him, and that the matter not stop at accusations brought against him by his adversaries with no established facts against him.

31.34.7.en: “Surely I would take it upon my shoulder.”

31.35.0.en: “I would bind it as a crown to me” [36].

31.35.1.en: Job asks for a public trial, reckoning that while being tried as a criminal he receives honor, and he considers the accusations leveled against him a crown that wreathes his head, because God will surely justify him!

31.36.0.en: “I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him” [37].

31.36.1.en: Righteous Job declares that he will hide nothing of the steps of his whole life. For he knew that his life bore witness to him as a prince and not as a criminal.

31.37.0.en: “If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain” [38].

31.37.1.en: In his certainty that he never wronged anyone, but showed tenderness as far as he could and gave constantly, he therefore asks them to look at the land, for it bears witness, it and its produce, to his love; it finds no single complaint against him, and neither weeps nor laments over any conduct of his.

31.37.2.en: * The earth does not sigh or grieve. What, then, does he mean by this? It is not that the earth truly (in the literal sense) sighs, but these lifeless things are offended by injustice, as the prophet says: [The earth shall be broken, and struck with terror] (Jer 4:28)(a). In any case the earth sighs every time we use its fruits unjustly.

31.38.0.en: St. John Chrysostom “If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life” [39].

31.38.1.en: “Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley.”

31.39.1.en: Job challenges his friends, saying that if he had wronged anyone and taken produce (wheat or barley) without paying the price, he would not grieve if those subject to him offered thorns and tares instead of grain for food and refreshment.

31.39.2.en: He affirms that if he were unjust he would not deserve to eat bread of wheat like the poorest of mankind, nor barley like the animals, but that men should offer him words sharp as thorns or worthless words like tares, since he would deserve only to be cast into the fire.

31.39.3.en: The words of Job in his dialogue with his friends are ended, and in his speech he felt that he was speaking in the presence of God; indeed he often directs his speech to God Himself, for he seeks God’s approval, not that a man should justify him.

31.39.4.en: Shine with Your light in my depths

31.39.5.en: * Grant me, with Your devout servant Job, to discover my depths.

31.39.6.en: I know the weight of my sins, but who can sanctify me but You?

31.39.7.en: Without You I am struck by the darkness that has reigned within me.

31.39.8.en: In You I am filled with hope for Your salvation, O You who shine upon me with Your glory!

31.39.9.en: You gave the face of Moses radiance; give my depths a radiance from You.

31.39.10.en: * I do not allow my eyes to look at a virgin.

31.39.11.en: But who gives my heart, my mind and my emotions a virgin purity but You?

31.39.12.en: You are my portion and my eternal inheritance; I possess You, so that the love of lust does not creep into my depths.

31.39.13.en: * You are the Searcher of hearts and reins; You know all my hidden secrets, not to condemn me but to sanctify me.

31.39.14.en: * You are the Truth; whoever possesses You does not make peace with falsehood, nor enters into dealings with the devil, the liar and the father of liars.

31.39.15.en: * The heavens are not clean in Your sight, and You charge Your angels with folly, so how shall I be justified before You?

31.39.16.en: Let me be weighed in the balance of Your love, and Your Cross will support me.

31.39.17.en: Let me put on Your free righteousness, that I may appear before the divine throne.

31.39.18.en: * In You I possess purity, tenderness and truth.

31.39.19.en: Then adultery will not come near my body, nor my soul!

31.39.20.en: I will respect every man, and see You in every person!

31.39.21.en: I will not care for wealth or authority, for You are my wealth and my glory!

31.39.22.en: I will love even my enemies and my opponents, and desire the peace of the whole world and its glory in You.

31.39.23.en: Let the world rise up against me, for I desire to wash its feet!

31.39.24.en: Finally, grant me, with righteous Job, that You may be my all!
